concrete_changes.before: Trauma is not an emotion. It is a syntax error in the grammar of autobiographical memory.
concrete_changes.after: Syntax gives me a way to ask about experiences that resist an ordinary before-and-after account. It is a metaphor for an inquiry into trauma, not a diagnosis of someone telling their story.

concrete_changes.before: This is not a metaphor about how trauma *feels*. It is a description of how trauma *encodes*.
concrete_changes.after: The syntax comparison cannot settle the biological account of memory encoding.

concrete_changes.before: This is why traumatic memories are re-experienced, not recalled. The subject position has been evacuated.
concrete_changes.after: A grammatical subject gives this reading something to look for: who can speak, in what tense, and under which conditions? It cannot describe every person's memory.

concrete_changes.before: You are not difficult. Your nervous system is running a threat-detection routine in a context where the threat has already passed. The error is not moral. It is grammatical.
concrete_changes.after: A remembered threat and a present situation can be difficult to separate. Calling this a grammatical problem must not become another way to decide, from outside, what someone is experiencing.

concrete_changes.before:
There are three approaches that actually repair the grammar, and each addresses a different layer of the encoding.

**Narrative exposure** functions as an external hippocampus. The listener — therapist, friend, witness — provides the temporal scaffolding that the traumatized person's own hippocampus cannot generate. *This happened. Then this. Then this.* The shift from present-tense intrusion to past-tense memory is not therapeutic poetry. It is a neurological recoding. The narrative container is rebuilt from the outside in.

**EMDR** — eye movement desensitization and reprocessing — re-establishes inter-hemispheric communication. The bilateral stimulation appears to restore communication between the left hemisphere's linguistic, sequential processing and the right hemisphere's sensory, spatial encoding. The sensory fragments find their way back into syntax. Francine Shapiro discovered this by accident, walking in a park, noticing that her own distressing memories lost their charge as her eyes moved. The mechanism is still debated, but the efficacy is not.

**Somatic completion** addresses the body first. The truncated fight-or-flight responses remain as procedural memory — muscle tension, held breath, braced abdomen. Peter Levine's *Waking the Tiger* (1997) documents how guiding the body through the incomplete biological arc — the shake, the run, the cry that was swallowed — updates the procedural memory before the declarative memory can be recompiled. The body must finish what it started. Narrative repair that skips this layer is architecture without a foundation.
concrete_changes.after:
Narrative exposure, EMDR and somatic approaches enter this discussion through different questions about telling, attending and bodily experience. Their mechanisms and uses cannot be derived from a syntax metaphor.

An external listener may help make room for a sequence without demanding a tidy account. That is the relation the compiler image lets me examine; calling the listener an external hippocampus would turn it into an unsupported biological identity.

The same limit applies to EMDR's bilateral stimulation. The claim that it reconnects linguistic and sensory hemispheres needs evidence of its own, rather than an attractive red-and-green brain diagram. Peter Levine's *Waking the Tiger* (1997) gives a source to examine for the language of incomplete response. It does not establish here that every body must finish a prescribed arc before a story can change.

The person remains more particular than the repair diagram. No one should have to produce a completed narrative to qualify for care.

concrete_changes.after: This three-part reading is a proposal for attention, not a test a survivor can fail.

concrete_changes.before: The question is not whether you can return to who you were before. The question is whether you can develop the authorship to redraw the map in your own syntax. The Quine holds: the repair succeeds when you no longer need the external compiler.
concrete_changes.after: The emergency ink may remain on the map. Authorship, in this image, includes the right to leave part of it unfinished and to decide who may read it.

concrete_changes.before:
## The Triad Governs

Kha — the observer — must re-establish itself without fusion. The witness must be rebuilt — not as dissociation, not as denial, but as the capacity to hold the event in awareness without becoming the event. This is the difference between *I was attacked* and *I am being attacked*. The subject returns to the sentence.

Ba — the body — must complete its arc. The substrate must be allowed to finish what threat interrupted. Not through catharsis, which is often just more observation trying to narrate its way out, but through the slow, specific discharge of held charge. The jaw unlocks. The diaphragm descends. The hands stop bracing for impact.

La — the resistance — is what makes the repair real. Without friction, there is no form. The work is not to dissolve the trauma but to metabolize it — to turn the energy of survival into the architecture of resilience. The scar is not a mistake. It is the record of a successful repair.

This three-part reading is a proposal for attention, not a test a survivor can fail. All witness and no body produces a person who can narrate their trauma with perfect clarity while their body still screams. All body and no witness produces a person who discharges somatically but cannot author the meaning of what they are discharging. All witness and body without resistance produces insight without weight — philosophy, not inhabitation.
concrete_changes.after:
## The Triad as Questions

Kha asks what can be observed without demanding a finished story. Ba keeps the person's particular bodily experience in the account. La asks what makes change difficult and what support is available.

Those questions offer no universal sequence of repair. A body need not complete a prescribed arc, discharge a specified charge or produce a narrative resolution before care can begin.
